Determine if $b\in \text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$ from the decomposition $b={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 10\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=10\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 6 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=-5.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-5.$ Substituting into the first equation gives 

$$
{x}_{1}+4(-5)=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=20.
$$

Since the system has a solution, we can conclude that $b\in \text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}.$

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $b$ as a linear combination of ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}20{a}_{1}+(-5){a}_{2} & =b \\ 20\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+(-5)\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=20\cdot (-5)=-100.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2974b131-4f18-559b-891b-6b98e368f920"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-2974b131-4f18-559b-891b-6b98e368f920" :answer-field/id #uuid "2974b131-4f18-559b-891b-6b98e368f920" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1a7a3f85-c316-5d92-9f90-b24c014d8770" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1a7a3f85-c316-5d92-9f90-b24c014d8770" "answer-8c1e9e25-575f-5bba-bb57-6864dc973a15" "answer-49efebb4-5b44-54d8-a642-d7be1bed4e5c" "answer-f486e66a-d479-5a8a-b1e9-cfb2602b755d" "answer-244d18d1-69c9-554a-801a-a1ee85e653f9"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1a7a3f85-c316-5d92-9f90-b24c014d8770" :answer/id #uuid "1a7a3f85-c316-5d92-9f90-b24c014d8770" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-100" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8c1e9e25-575f-5bba-bb57-6864dc973a15" :answer/id #uuid "8c1e9e25-575f-5bba-bb57-6864dc973a15" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-49efebb4-5b44-54d8-a642-d7be1bed4e5c" :answer/id #uuid "49efebb4-5b44-54d8-a642-d7be1bed4e5c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "100" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f486e66a-d479-5a8a-b1e9-cfb2602b755d" :answer/id #uuid "f486e66a-d479-5a8a-b1e9-cfb2602b755d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "20" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-244d18d1-69c9-554a-801a-a1ee85e653f9" :answer/id #uuid "244d18d1-69c9-554a-801a-a1ee85e653f9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "b\notin \text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-c75c18ab-94b6-560b-bd47-66c76f099710" :question/id #uuid "c75c18ab-94b6-560b-bd47-66c76f099710" :question/math-academy-id "q-105215" :question/problem "The vectors ${a}_{1}$, ${a}_{2}$, and $b$ are given below. Determine if $b\in \text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$ from the decomposition $b={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}=3 \\ -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}3 & -6 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The second row of the augmented matrix now corresponds to the equation $0{x}_{1}+0{x}_{2}=1,$ which has no solution.

So, there are no values of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $b$ does *not* lie in $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields "question-cdba03e5-45ad-5856-b84f-f9bccefe0c86" :question/id #uuid "cdba03e5-45ad-5856-b84f-f9bccefe0c86" :question/math-academy-id "q-105242" :question/problem "Find the values of $k$ such that the vector $b$ lies in $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 18 \\ 39\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -6 \\ k\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 18 \\ 39\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -6 \\ k\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+7{x}_{2}=-3 \\ 3{x}_{1}+18{x}_{2}=-6 \\ 5{x}_{1}+39{x}_{2}=k\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 7 & -3 \\ 3 & 18 & -6 \\ 5 & 39 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 7 & -3 \\ 0 & -3 & 3 \\ 5 & 39 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 7 & -3 \\ 0 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 4 & k+15\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 7 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 4 & k+15\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 7 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & k+19\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The third row of the augmented matrix now corresponds to the equation $0{x}_{1}+0{x}_{2}=k+19.$ Therefore, the system has a solution only if

$$
0=k+19\,⇒\,k=-19.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8e5fe0f3-2bfd-5489-af0f-1a776954c9bd"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8e5fe0f3-2bfd-5489-af0f-1a776954c9bd" :answer-field/id #uuid "8e5fe0f3-2bfd-5489-af0f-1a776954c9bd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-8b330e4c-1039-5eb3-95e3-86ecad96d372" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d5866e44-8aa4-58d9-b2ef-ad9461dd3c47" "answer-8b330e4c-1039-5eb3-95e3-86ecad96d372" "answer-18da01e3-a753-5c12-b310-e49dbac1352a" "answer-c506c166-ea56-5484-9ce8-55f2a4ef6b2b" "answer-94545aa5-65f2-555f-8c83-9dc00de7552e"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d5866e44-8aa4-58d9-b2ef-ad9461dd3c47" :answer/id #uuid "d5866e44-8aa4-58d9-b2ef-ad9461dd3c47" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-15" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8b330e4c-1039-5eb3-95e3-86ecad96d372" :answer/id #uuid "8b330e4c-1039-5eb3-95e3-86ecad96d372" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-19" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-18da01e3-a753-5c12-b310-e49dbac1352a" :answer/id #uuid "18da01e3-a753-5c12-b310-e49dbac1352a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "13" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c506c166-ea56-5484-9ce8-55f2a4ef6b2b" :answer/id #uuid "c506c166-ea56-5484-9ce8-55f2a4ef6b2b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "17" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-94545aa5-65f2-555f-8c83-9dc00de7552e" :answer/id #uuid "94545aa5-65f2-555f-8c83-9dc00de7552e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "21" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-f6e087fb-be43-5d06-8b0f-af7c87178067" :question/id #uuid "f6e087fb-be43-5d06-8b0f-af7c87178067" :question/math-academy-id "q-105241" :question/problem "Find the values of $k$ such that the vector $b$ lies in $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 4 \\ -12\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ -6\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3 \\ k\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 4 \\ -12\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ -6\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3 \\ k\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-8{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=5 \\ 4{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=-3 \\ -12{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}=k\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}-8 & -3 & 5 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ -12 & -6 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & -3 \\ -8 & -3 & 5 \\ -12 & -6 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ -12 & -6 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & k-9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The third row of the augmented matrix now corresponds to the equation $0{x}_{1}+0{x}_{2}=k-9.$ Therefore, the system has a solution only if

$$
0=k-9\,⇒\,k=9.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2d064b98-7b87-5c7b-a6e2-625fb2a9f2b1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-5b9c3557-0777-5517-a4eb-de326b8ca141" :question/id #uuid "5b9c3557-0777-5517-a4eb-de326b8ca141" :question/math-academy-id "q-74609" :question/problem "Determine if the vector $u$ lies on the plane $Π:r=sb+tc$, $t,s\in R$, where  $b=⟨-1,4,3⟩$, $c=⟨2,-6,-4⟩$, and  $u=⟨3,-7,-4⟩.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $u=sb+tc.$" :question/worked-solution "By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ -4\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -7 \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-s+2t=3 \\ 4s-6t=-7 \\ 3s-4t=-4\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & -6 & -7 \\ 3 & -4 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 5 \\ 3 & -4 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}-s+2t=3 \\ 2t=5 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
2t=5\,⟹\,t=\frac{5}{2}.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-s+2t & =3 \\ -s+2(\frac{5}{2}) & =3 \\ -s+5 & =3 \\ -s & =-2 \\ s & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=2,\,t=\frac{5}{2},$ we conclude that $u$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
u=2b+\frac{5}{2}c.
$$

$$
U = \left\{ x_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \: : \: x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R} \right\}.
$$

The set $U$ is also called the **linear span** of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ and is denoted by $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}.$ We say that $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ are the **generators** of $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}.$

For example, let's find the linear span generated by the following vectors:
![](images/55/55c749dccc54c252b9120f148e383f395c09fb4cd4bec0e1cce8ed441ecb6199.svg)

From the definition of linear span, we know that if $\mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ then $\mathbf{b}$ must take the form

$$
\mathbf{b} = x_1\mathbf{a_1} + x_2\mathbf{a_2}
$$

 for some $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}b & ={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the linear span of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ is
![](images/21/2181b471f34906eeaea7889abbba37c797a2f9624cee455b43b00fc048247cd1.svg)

Geometrically, $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}$ can be viewed as the plane $\Pi$ that passes through the origin and is parallel to the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ as shown below.

![](images/d5/d5b202475e0bc3ebb07df1f07bab72e9e74b13a99196c2a8a5adb624a7534a03.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121036 :tutorial/content "The linear span of vectors can be interpreted geometrically as the points in space that can be reached by adding multiples of those vectors.

- The span of a single nonzero vector is a *line* through the origin. More precisely, if $\mathbf{a} \neq \mathbf{0},$ then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a} \}$ determines the *line* with direction vector $\mathbf{a}$ that passes through the origin. For instance, if
![](images/dd/ddef437718d3a11811da02a17e2207d75e2d1852eeada67ab494af45b2a655e2.svg)
then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a} \}$ represents the line $l$ *spanned* by $\mathbf{a}\mathbin{:}$

![](images/08/080aa6203494e915e28c491a3d86176f7ba634bcbdfe40b094c07d85fb29bb69.png)

- The span of two non-parallel vectors is a *plane* through the origin. More precisely, if $\mathbf{a} \not\parallel \mathbf{b}$ ($\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are not parallel), then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \}$ determines the *plane* with direction vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ that passes through the origin. For instance, if
![](images/1f/1f92378ff1d1409f0928caa4b3ce98861784d0f2aa51dd1eda30e8877a0134ff.svg)
then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \}$  represents the plane $\Pi$ *spanned* by $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

![](images/56/5606535bd91eb35745a9852ceb451720339105f5a97fb66ccfcb1164ecd55ffd.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186120046 :activity/expected-seconds 960.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

Determine if $b\in \text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$ from the decomposition $b={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 10\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=10\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 6 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=-5.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-5.$ Substituting into the first equation gives 

$$
{x}_{1}+4(-5)=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=20.
$$

Since the system has a solution, we can conclude that $b\in \text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}.$

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $b$ as a linear combination of ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}20{a}_{1}+(-5){a}_{2} & =b \\ 20\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+(-5)\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=20\cdot (-5)=-100.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2974b131-4f18-559b-891b-6b98e368f920"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-2974b131-4f18-559b-891b-6b98e368f920" :answer-field/id #uuid "2974b131-4f18-559b-891b-6b98e368f920" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1a7a3f85-c316-5d92-9f90-b24c014d8770" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1a7a3f85-c316-5d92-9f90-b24c014d8770" "answer-8c1e9e25-575f-5bba-bb57-6864dc973a15" "answer-49efebb4-5b44-54d8-a642-d7be1bed4e5c" "answer-f486e66a-d479-5a8a-b1e9-cfb2602b755d" "answer-244d18d1-69c9-554a-801a-a1ee85e653f9"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1a7a3f85-c316-5d92-9f90-b24c014d8770" :answer/id #uuid "1a7a3f85-c316-5d92-9f90-b24c014d8770" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-100" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8c1e9e25-575f-5bba-bb57-6864dc973a15" :answer/id #uuid "8c1e9e25-575f-5bba-bb57-6864dc973a15" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-49efebb4-5b44-54d8-a642-d7be1bed4e5c" :answer/id #uuid "49efebb4-5b44-54d8-a642-d7be1bed4e5c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "100" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f486e66a-d479-5a8a-b1e9-cfb2602b755d" :answer/id #uuid "f486e66a-d479-5a8a-b1e9-cfb2602b755d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "20" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-244d18d1-69c9-554a-801a-a1ee85e653f9" :answer/id #uuid "244d18d1-69c9-554a-801a-a1ee85e653f9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "b\notin \text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-c75c18ab-94b6-560b-bd47-66c76f099710" :question/id #uuid "c75c18ab-94b6-560b-bd47-66c76f099710" :question/math-academy-id "q-105215" :question/problem "The vectors ${a}_{1}$, ${a}_{2}$, and $b$ are given below. Determine if $b\in \text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$ from the decomposition $b={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}=3 \\ -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}3 & -6 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The second row of the augmented matrix now corresponds to the equation $0{x}_{1}+0{x}_{2}=1,$ which has no solution.

So, there are no values of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $b$ does *not* lie in $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields "question-5b9c3557-0777-5517-a4eb-de326b8ca141" :question/id #uuid "5b9c3557-0777-5517-a4eb-de326b8ca141" :question/math-academy-id "q-74609" :question/problem "Determine if the vector $u$ lies on the plane $Π:r=sb+tc$, $t,s\in R$, where  $b=⟨-1,4,3⟩$, $c=⟨2,-6,-4⟩$, and  $u=⟨3,-7,-4⟩.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $u=sb+tc.$" :question/worked-solution "By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ -4\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -7 \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-s+2t=3 \\ 4s-6t=-7 \\ 3s-4t=-4\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & -6 & -7 \\ 3 & -4 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 5 \\ 3 & -4 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}-s+2t=3 \\ 2t=5 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
2t=5\,⟹\,t=\frac{5}{2}.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-s+2t & =3 \\ -s+2(\frac{5}{2}) & =3 \\ -s+5 & =3 \\ -s & =-2 \\ s & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=2,\,t=\frac{5}{2},$ we conclude that $u$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
u=2b+\frac{5}{2}c.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=2\cdot \frac{5}{2}=5.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fe4e956c-1b1f-5312-af0b-3bb85188fdbd"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-fe4e956c-1b1f-5312-af0b-3bb85188fdbd" :answer-field/id #uuid "fe4e956c-1b1f-5312-af0b-3bb85188fdbd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-31aa51c7-7bbf-539a-8251-ca7e5420f8e3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-404186fe-c6bf-5419-b373-a5941944a534" "answer-ffbc367b-e607-5dad-b444-946e25112421" "answer-31aa51c7-7bbf-539a-8251-ca7e5420f8e3" "answer-a5aeef05-ac8e-5ffc-b5cd-7dab5e605fc9" "answer-cb1bdf10-0234-549d-b4c6-dcf3de7b6fdc"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-404186fe-c6bf-5419-b373-a5941944a534" :answer/id #uuid "404186fe-c6bf-5419-b373-a5941944a534" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ffbc367b-e607-5dad-b444-946e25112421" :answer/id #uuid "ffbc367b-e607-5dad-b444-946e25112421" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-31aa51c7-7bbf-539a-8251-ca7e5420f8e3" :answer/id #uuid "31aa51c7-7bbf-539a-8251-ca7e5420f8e3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a5aeef05-ac8e-5ffc-b5cd-7dab5e605fc9" :answer/id #uuid "a5aeef05-ac8e-5ffc-b5cd-7dab5e605fc9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cb1bdf10-0234-549d-b4c6-dcf3de7b6fdc" :answer/id #uuid "cb1bdf10-0234-549d-b4c6-dcf3de7b6fdc" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$u$ does not lie on $Π$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121035 :tutorial/content "Given two vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ the set of all possible linear combinations of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ is

$$
U = \left\{ x_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \: : \: x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R} \right\}.
$$

The set $U$ is also called the **linear span** of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ and is denoted by $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}.$ We say that $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ are the **generators** of $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}.$

For example, let's find the linear span generated by the following vectors:
![](images/55/55c749dccc54c252b9120f148e383f395c09fb4cd4bec0e1cce8ed441ecb6199.svg)

From the definition of linear span, we know that if $\mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ then $\mathbf{b}$ must take the form

$$
\mathbf{b} = x_1\mathbf{a_1} + x_2\mathbf{a_2}
$$

 for some $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}b & ={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the linear span of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ is
![](images/21/2181b471f34906eeaea7889abbba37c797a2f9624cee455b43b00fc048247cd1.svg)

Geometrically, $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}$ can be viewed as the plane $\Pi$ that passes through the origin and is parallel to the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ as shown below.

![](images/d5/d5b202475e0bc3ebb07df1f07bab72e9e74b13a99196c2a8a5adb624a7534a03.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121036 :tutorial/content "The linear span of vectors can be interpreted geometrically as the points in space that can be reached by adding multiples of those vectors.

- The span of a single nonzero vector is a *line* through the origin. More precisely, if $\mathbf{a} \neq \mathbf{0},$ then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a} \}$ determines the *line* with direction vector $\mathbf{a}$ that passes through the origin. For instance, if
![](images/dd/ddef437718d3a11811da02a17e2207d75e2d1852eeada67ab494af45b2a655e2.svg)
then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a} \}$ represents the line $l$ *spanned* by $\mathbf{a}\mathbin{:}$

![](images/08/080aa6203494e915e28c491a3d86176f7ba634bcbdfe40b094c07d85fb29bb69.png)

- The span of two non-parallel vectors is a *plane* through the origin. More precisely, if $\mathbf{a} \not\parallel \mathbf{b}$ ($\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are not parallel), then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \}$ determines the *plane* with direction vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ that passes through the origin. For instance, if
![](images/1f/1f92378ff1d1409f0928caa4b3ce98861784d0f2aa51dd1eda30e8877a0134ff.svg)
then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \}$  represents the plane $\Pi$ *spanned* by $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=-5.\end{aligned}

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-5.$ Substituting into the first equation gives 

$$

$$

["question-5b9c3557-0777-5517-a4eb-de326b8ca141" :question/math-academy-id "q-74609"] ["question-5b9c3557-0777-5517-a4eb-de326b8ca141" :question/problem "Determine if the vector $u$ lies on the plane $Π:r=sb+tc$, $t,s\in R$, where  $b=⟨-1,4,3⟩$, $c=⟨2,-6,-4⟩$, and  $u=⟨3,-7,-4⟩.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $u=sb+tc.$"] ["question-5b9c3557-0777-5517-a4eb-de326b8ca141" :question/worked-solution "By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ -4\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -7 \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-s+2t=3 \\ 4s-6t=-7 \\ 3s-4t=-4\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & -6 & -7 \\ 3 & -4 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 5 \\ 3 & -4 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}-s+2t=3 \\ 2t=5 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
2t=5\,⟹\,t=\frac{5}{2}.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-s+2t & =3 \\ -s+2(\frac{5}{2}) & =3 \\ -s+5 & =3 \\ -s & =-2 \\ s & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=2,\,t=\frac{5}{2},$ we conclude that $u$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
u=2b+\frac{5}{2}c.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=2\cdot \frac{5}{2}=5.$"] ["question-5b9c3557-0777-5517-a4eb-de326b8ca141" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-fe4e956c-1b1f-5312-af0b-3bb85188fdbd" "answer-field-fe4e956c-1b1f-5312-af0b-3bb85188fdbd"] [17592186119809 :knowledge-point/questions "question-5b9c3557-0777-5517-a4eb-de326b8ca141"] [17592186121035 :tutorial/content "Given two vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ the set of all possible linear combinations of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ is

$$
U = \left\{ x_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \: : \: x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R} \right\}.
$$

The set $U$ is also called the **linear span** of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ and is denoted by $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}.$ We say that $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ are the **generators** of $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}.$

For example, let's find the linear span generated by the following vectors:
![](images/55/55c749dccc54c252b9120f148e383f395c09fb4cd4bec0e1cce8ed441ecb6199.svg)

From the definition of linear span, we know that if $\mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ then $\mathbf{b}$ must take the form

$$
\mathbf{b} = x_1\mathbf{a_1} + x_2\mathbf{a_2}
$$

 for some $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}b & ={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the linear span of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ is
![](images/21/2181b471f34906eeaea7889abbba37c797a2f9624cee455b43b00fc048247cd1.svg)

Geometrically, $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}$ can be viewed as the plane $\Pi$ that passes through the origin and is parallel to the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ as shown below.

$$
{\begin{aligned}s+2t=2 \\ 4s+4t=10 \\ 5s+6t=12\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 4 & 4 & 10 \\ 5 & 6 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 \\ 5 & 6 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-5{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}s+2t=2 \\ -4t=2 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
-4t = 2 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad t = -\dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}s+2t & =2 \\ s+2(-\frac{1}{2}) & =2 \\ s-1 & =2 \\ s & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find the values of $k$ such that the vector $b$ lies in $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -4\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5 \\ k\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -4\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5 \\ k\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=3 \\ {x}_{2}=5 \\ -4{x}_{1}+7{x}_{2}=k\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 \\ -4 & 7 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & k+12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & k-3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The third row of the augmented matrix now corresponds to the equation $0{x}_{1}+0{x}_{2}=k-3.$ Therefore, the system has a solution only if

$$
0=k-3\,⇒\,k=3.

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186120676 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121035 :tutorial/content "Given two vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ the set of all possible linear combinations of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ is

$$
U = \left\{ x_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \: : \: x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R} \right\}.
$$

The set $U$ is also called the **linear span** of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ and is denoted by $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}.$ We say that $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ are the **generators** of $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}.$

For example, let's find the linear span generated by the following vectors:

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

From the definition of linear span, we know that if $\mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ then $\mathbf{b}$ must take the form

$$
\mathbf{b} = x_1\mathbf{a_1} + x_2\mathbf{a_2}
$$

 for some $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}b & ={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the linear span of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

Geometrically, $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}$ can be viewed as the plane $\Pi$ that passes through the origin and is parallel to the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ as shown below.

- The span of a single nonzero vector is a *line* through the origin. More precisely, if $\mathbf{a} \neq \mathbf{0},$ then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a} \}$ determines the *line* with direction vector $\mathbf{a}$ that passes through the origin. For instance, if

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a} \}$ represents the line $l$ *spanned* by $\mathbf{a}\mathbin{:}$

![](images/08/080aa6203494e915e28c491a3d86176f7ba634bcbdfe40b094c07d85fb29bb69.png)

- The span of two non-parallel vectors is a *plane* through the origin. More precisely, if $\mathbf{a} \not\parallel \mathbf{b}$ ($\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are not parallel), then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \}$ determines the *plane* with direction vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ that passes through the origin. For instance, if

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \}$  represents the plane $\Pi$ *spanned* by $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

vectors can be interpreted geometrically as the points in space that can be reached by adding multiples of those vectors.

- The span of a single nonzero vector is a *line* through the origin. More precisely, if $\mathbf{a} \neq \mathbf{0},$ then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a} \}$ determines the *line* with direction vector $\mathbf{a}$ that passes through the origin. For instance, if

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a} \}$ represents the line $l$ *spanned* by $\mathbf{a}\mathbin{:}$

![](images/08/080aa6203494e915e28c491a3d86176f7ba634bcbdfe40b094c07d85fb29bb69.png)

- The span of two non-parallel vectors is a *plane* through the origin. More precisely, if $\mathbf{a} \not\parallel \mathbf{b}$ ($\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are not parallel), then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \}$ determines the *plane* with direction vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ that passes through the origin. For instance, if

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \}$  represents the plane $\Pi$ *spanned* by $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

machine learning.
This course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.
On completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.
Students then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.
As part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.
Students will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.
The course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.
A solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.
Students also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.
Students work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.
On the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.
Students extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.
The course concludes with parametric inference, focusing on point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals, which form the statistical foundation for many machine learning
